column4: The section sets a person's visible state against the Lord's knowledge of the inward person; this ayah says hidden speech and spoken speech are equally within God's knowledge, including what is in breasts. Ayah 67:14 completes the sequence with its question about the Creator's knowledge.

The section's 100:9 asks whether a person knows, then 100:11 names the Lord al-Khabir; this ayah asks whether the Creator knows and ends with اللطيف الخبير. Ayah 67:13 supplies the preceding hidden/open speech and breast detail.

The section says 100:7 makes the person a witness to his own ingratitude; here the person is عَلَىٰ نَفْسِهِ بَصِيرَةٌ, a clear-sighted witness against himself. Ayat 75:13 and 75:15 frame this self-knowledge with the later report and failed excuses.

Where 100:9 asks whether the person knows what the resurrection discloses, this ayah says he will be informed of what he sent ahead and left behind. Ayat 75:14-15 add the self-witness and excuses that the section also develops.
The section calls the root ش ه د a witness's presence, knowledge and announcement, and notes its tongue sense; here tongues, hands and feet testify against people about their deeds.

The section's root ش ه د and its tongue-as-witness sense become bodily speech here: people ask their skins why they testified, and the skins answer that God made them speak. Ayat 41:20 and 41:22 continue the scene with other body parts and the people's mistaken belief about concealment.

The section moves from a person's seeing to the disclosure of his inward state; here hearing, sight and skins testify against their owners. Ayah 41:21 gives the skins' reply, completing this row's bodily-witness scene.

The section asks whether a person knows what will be disclosed and says the Lord knows the people themselves; here the condemned say they could not hide from their own hearing, sight and skins, exposing their failed account of concealment. Ayat 41:21 and 41:23 explain the testimony and their mistaken thought about God.

The section contrasts a person's limited knowledge with the Lord's full inward knowledge; this ayah says their assumption about their Lord ruined them. Ayah 41:22 states the assumption, while 41:21 supplies the bodily testimony that disproves it.

The section's witness is present and reported, with the tongue as its instrument; here mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet bear witness to what people earned, making the body disclose the person.
The section says the final knowledge concerns the people themselves and their inward reality; this ayah names what the self whispers and God's nearness to the person as the ground of that knowledge.

The section's movement from what a person sees to what the Lord knows inwardly is answered by this removal of a covering: the person's sight is sharp on that Day. Ayat 50:16-18 have already named the whisper and its recording, making the disclosure concrete.

The section explicitly applies 100:11's divine knowledge of people to one who outwardly professes faith but turns away under hardship; this ayah asks whether God knows best what is in the worlds' breasts in that very setting.
The section says the Lord knows people inwardly even when their outward condition is all a person sees; here people fold their breasts to hide, but God knows what they conceal and disclose.
The section contrasts seen or announced matters with what lies inside; this ayah says that whether speech is aloud, concealed, or more hidden, God knows it.
The section moves from human sight to the Lord's knowledge of the person within; this ayah specifies both a treacherous glance and what breasts conceal, pairing the outward eye with inward knowledge.
The section's last claim is that the Lord is fully aware of the people themselves; this ayah says He knows what their breasts conceal and reveal.
The section says a person witnesses his state but does not grasp its outcome, while the Lord is al-Khabir; this ayah says no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, whereas God is عليم خبير.

The section gives خ ب ر the secondary dictionary sense of testing and reaching the inward reality; this ayah says God has tested the believers' hearts for God-consciousness, making an inner quality known through a trial.
The section distinguishes visible state from what is inside the person; this ayah says the trial was to test what was in breasts and purify what was in hearts.
The section names الخبرة as testing and connects خبر to knowledge of an affair's inward reality; this ayah says God will test people and test their أخبار, joining trial to what is learned about them.

The section's dictionary branch calls experience testing; this ayah asks whether people think they can claim belief without being tested. Ayah 29:3 completes the point by saying the trial distinguishes truthful claimants from liars.

The section says an inner reality is reached through testing; this ayah says God makes evident the truthful and the lying through people's trials. Ayah 29:2 states the test that brings this distinction out.
The section says 100:10 gathers what is in breasts and 100:11 makes the Lord's knowledge of people explicit; this ayah names the Day when hidden things are exposed, تُبْلَى السَّرَائِرُ.
The section contrasts what a person sees outwardly with what the Lord knows inwardly; this ayah describes the Day when people are exposed and nothing about them remains hidden.

The section's question in 100:9 names the graves being scattered; this ayah repeats the same grave scene, إِذَا الْقُبُورُ بُعْثِرَتْ. Ayah 82:5 completes it by saying each soul knows what it sent ahead and left behind.

The section asks whether the person knows when the graves are scattered and the chests' contents gathered; this ayah answers with what each soul will know about what it sent ahead and left behind. Ayah 82:4 supplies the preceding grave-scattering scene.

The section asks what a person knows when the resurrection discloses what was inside; after the scrolls are unrolled and the other scenes of that Day, this ayah says every soul will know what it brought.
The section explicitly links the earth's report on that Day to the root خ ب ر in its final word; this ayah says the earth will tell its أَخْبَارَهَا, its reports.
The section cites the earth telling its reports in 99:4; this next ayah says its reporting follows its Lord's inspiration, completing the image's speaking earth.

The section asks whether a person knows when the graves are scattered and his inner state disclosed; this ayah shows people emerging in groups to be shown their deeds. Ayat 99:7-8 specify what each person sees.

The section turns on what becomes known on the Day of resurrection; this ayah says whoever did an atom's weight of good will see it. Ayah 99:6 gives the people's presentation, and 99:8 states the matching rule for evil.

The section asks about knowledge at resurrection; this ayah says whoever did an atom's weight of evil will see it. Ayah 99:6 stages people being shown their deeds, and 99:7 gives the corresponding good deed.

The section says that what is in people will be disclosed; here the record is set down, people find their deeds present, and the book leaves out neither small nor great. This gives the day of disclosure an exact account of actions.
The section describes a person as witness to himself; this ayah tells him to read his book and says, كَفَىٰ بِنَفْسِكَ الْيَوْمَ عَلَيْكَ حَسِيبًا, making the self itself the day's reckoner.

The section says the Lord knows people even when they do not grasp their own state; this ayah says He will gather them and inform them of what they did, though they had forgotten it, while God had counted it.
The section traces sight and hearing toward knowledge and accountability; this ayah forbids following what one does not know, then names hearing, sight and heart as each answerable for its use.

The section's question أَفَلَا يَعْلَمُ asks what the person knows before the Day of disclosure; this ayah repeats that rhetorical form and answers that God sees, reversing the assumption that the visible act escapes notice.

The section says the root ش ه د includes knowing and reporting, and that a person is witness against himself; this ayah commands witnesses to uphold justice even when testimony is against themselves or their parents and kin.
The section treats testimony as a decisive report that joins knowing and informing; this ayah forbids concealing testimony and locates the sin of concealment in the heart.
The section says people are witnesses to their own state; this ayah has people testify against themselves that they were unbelievers, in the address on the Day of gathering.

The section says testimony combines knowledge and informing, while the Lord knows what humans cannot; here Joseph's brothers say they testify only to what they know and are not guardians of the unseen, marking the limit of a human report.

The section names the tongue as an instrument of witness and says testimony is a decisive report; this ayah reverses that ideal with people passing words by their tongues and saying what they have no knowledge of.

The section says testimony is a decisive report; after the tongue-borne claim in 24:15, this ayah asks why its hearers did not call it a grave slander, marking the boundary between testimony and unsupported speech.

The section calls testimony a decisive report; this ayah warns that a report from an unreliable source must be checked, lest people be harmed in ignorance. It specifies how a report becomes knowledge rather than treating every utterance as certain.
The section says a person is witness to his own ingratitude; this ayah says people recognize God's favor and then deny it, making recognition and denial coexist in the same person.
The section says the root ء ن س can mean seeing and connects knowing to خبر; this ayah joins them in Moses' words, إِنِّي آنَسْتُ نَارًا ... بِخَبَرٍ, perceiving a fire and going to bring news.
The section gives ء ن س the sense of perceiving by sight; Moses says إِنِّي آنَسْتُ نَارًا and goes to obtain a report or a firebrand, joining perception to what can be learned from it.
The section's named root ء ن س includes seeing; Moses says إِنِّي آنَسْتُ نَارًا, perceiving a fire before approaching it for a brand or guidance.

The section says a person sees his state while the Lord is witness and knows him; this ayah promises signs on the horizons and within people until truth is clear, then asks whether it is not enough that the Lord is witness over everything.
The section turns from what is seen outwardly to knowledge of the person himself; this ayah directs attention to one's own self and asks, أَفَلَا تُبْصِرُونَ, will you not see?

The section's question concerns what becomes known after resurrection; here the guilty lower their heads and say they now see and hear, but ask to be sent back, staging recognition after the point when it could guide them.
The section traces seeing and hearing into knowledge and names the person's ingratitude; this ayah says God gave people hearing, sight and hearts, yet little thanks they give.

The section says the root ء ن س covers seeing and hearing as ways toward knowing; this ayah says people emerge knowing nothing, then receive hearing, sight and hearts, linking perception to acquired knowledge.
The section moves from seeing and hearing toward knowledge; this ayah says God made hearing, sight and hearts, yet little gratitude is shown, joining perception to the person's response.
The section connects the senses with knowing the person; this ayah says God formed and breathed into the human, then gave hearing, sight and hearts, with little thanks in response.

The section follows seeing and hearing into knowledge; this ayah reverses that path by describing people with hearts that do not understand, eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear, despite having those faculties.
The section distinguishes what a person knows from what lies beyond him; Jacob tells his sons that he knows from God what they do not know, an explicit boundary between his insight and theirs.
The section says the Lord knows people inwardly while a person does not know what lies ahead; this ayah says no action, however small or great, escapes the Lord's knowledge or the clear record.
